item.title: Democrats begin high-stakes search for next House general counsel
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
It may be the most important decision Hakeem Jeffries makes when, as expected, he takes the speaker’s gavel in January and ignites a long-awaited constitutional clash with President Donald Trump: the selection of the House’s top lawyer. The House general counsel will be the muscle behind the chamber’s legal strategy to shatter Trump’s anticipated stonewalling, its gatekeeper to ensure only winnable fights end up in court, and its shield against a Justice Department that has already tried and failed to indict several Democratic members. And if the House pursues a third impeachment against Trump, its lawyer will be tasked with leading the chamber into the rarely litigated breach. That daunting job description comes with an even more ambitious goal: reasserting Congress’ power to check the president and reversing what Democrats see as the executive branch’s slow march toward autocracy under one-party rule. Democrats have been huddling for weeks to chart this approach — even before recapturing the House majority — meeting with lawyers steeped in the precepts of congressional power so they’re ready come Jan. 3. Jeffries and his top allies have not yet settled on a final candidate but view the choice as a crucial priority, according to a person familiar with the caucus deliberations, granted anonymity to share private conversations. The Democratic leader is also invested in restructuring and beefing up the House counsel’s office after years of Republican leadership uninterested in probing Trump administration excesses, the person said. Typically, speakers have appointed House counsels within several weeks of the start of a new session. Discussions about the next Congress’ oversight, including the role of House counsel, are well underway, said Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), who is slated to chair the Judiciary Committee. “There are some impressive and road-tested lawyers for the people who have surfaced over the last couple of years,” Raskin said. “We need lawyers who are ready and willing to go and fight, people who have devoted their lives to the Constitution. … We’re going to stand up for Congress against both the executive branch and the Supreme Court.” Raskin, a constitutional lawyer, said he’d had “terrific conversations” with Jeffries — a lawyer himself — about the House “flexing our muscle” to restore Congress’ place as “the preeminent branch.” Most of Jeffries’ immediate predecessors have been seasoned congressional appropriators, schooled in arcane fiscal matters that are often the lifeblood of the House’s work. Jeffries, though, rose to leadership via the House Judiciary Committee, which focuses on broader constitutional questions, the separation of powers and democratic principles that have been under strain in the Trump era. Jeffries, allies note, was one of the designated House prosecutors during Trump’s first impeachment, a perspective they say informs his thinking about Congress’ role as a check on the president. The conversations include ensuring a cohesive legal strategy between the House’s lead lawyer and the attorneys who will help guide the chamber’s investigators on the Judiciary and Oversight Committees. They’re already signaling their intent to investigate corruption allegations against Trump and his family, Trump’s use of the pardon power , ICE’s mass deportation campaign, the Justice Department’s targeting of Trump’s perceived political adversaries, efforts by Trump aides to unilaterally withhold funding appropriated by Congress and the administration’s handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files. A spokesperson for Jeffries did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Breaking through the stonewall Each telegraphed probe could prompt resistance from the administration, leading to court battles that could define the boundaries of the separation of powers in new ways. But those battles take time. Former House counsels say the incoming majority must be prepared to crank out its subpoenas as quickly as possible. “The House must have the ability to prevail when the law and facts are on its side and overcome what are likely to be extremely broad invocations of executive privilege,” said Thomas Spulak, one of the 11 people who has served as House counsel since the modern role was established in the 1970s. Though Democrats are projecting a tsunami of subpoenas, House veterans caution that it could take at least a month before committees are organized and prepared to launch investigations. The panels must wait for the minority party — newly led by Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio), a prominent Trump ally — to appoint members to the committees as well. Judges typically demand that lawmakers seek to compromise with the executive branch before they rush into court to enforce subpoenas, a time-consuming step that often moves slower than a two-year election cycle can bear. Raskin nodded to that requirement. “I do want to presume, even against all evidence, that there will be some lawful compliance on the side of the Trump administration," he said in an interview Monday. During their last run atop the House, Trump ordered his aides to resist all congressional subpoenas. A similar blanket rejection next year could help lawmakers sidestep that lengthy period of “accommodation” that courts prefer. Jeffries also has an advantage that his Democratic predecessor, Nancy Pelosi, did not: an apparent glidepath to the speaker’s gavel. That luxury, plus a historically large majority, will give Jeffries room to prepare his plans in advance and little fear of intraparty resistance that could derail them. Knowing that Trump will attempt to run out the clock on their probes — his universal strategy to foil his investigators — Democrats are preparing to squeeze the administration by pursuing third-party witnesses , like companies that have relationships with Trump or his family, or whistleblowers who give lawmakers leverage to demand information. “Often the best tactics are to find and protect willing witnesses, like John Dean during Watergate, or private witnesses not within the executive branch, like Elon Musk,” said Charles Tiefer, who spent 11 years in the House counsel’s office, including two as the top lawyer. Raskin said this strategy is already underway. “We have already heard from a whole bunch of whistleblowers,” he said. “We have lots of tips about things happening, everybody they’ve worked with in the private sector on various corrupt schemes, people who’ve been shaken down by them. We will be adamant about getting the information we need in order to legislate.” A shield against Trump admin investigations More than at any other time in recent memory, the House counsel is likely to be asked to act as a shield as much as a sword. The Justice Department has tried and failed to prosecute several Democratic lawmakers for encouraging U.S. troops to disregard illegal orders. And federal investigators recently seized the cellphone of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) in an immigration probe, raising separation of powers concerns that could require the House to intervene. More recently, Trump has taken explicit aim at House investigators, saying they should “ go to jail ” for their vows to conduct aggressive investigations of the president’s allies. Last week, he ordered, via social media, his Justice Department to “look into” lawmakers’ investigative letters, which he called a “criminal act.” Attorney General Todd Blanche fueled that message when he said on CNN Sunday that “there could be” investigations into Democrats who conduct oversight of the Trump administration. Blanche appeared more conciliatory during a Monday press conference when asked about congressional investigations: “Congress has oversight authority. It always has,” he said. “We’re not going to stop working with Congress or allowing them to conduct their oversight responsibilities.” In recent years, the House counsel has waded into criminal probes that have ensnared lawmakers to ensure that Congress’ constitutional immunity from executive branch pressure and scrutiny is protected. Most recently, the chamber — with bipartisan backing — encouraged a federal appeals court to sharply limit prosecutors’ ability to access the cellphone of Rep. Scott Perry (R-Pa.), which was seized during an investigation into Trump’s effort to overturn the 2020 election. Lessons from the Jan. 6 committee The last House counsel for Democrats, Doug Letter, became a prominent figure during one of the most successful oversight operations in modern history: the Jan. 6 select committee, which investigated Trump’s effort to subvert the 2020 election and the attack on Congress that ensued. Letter fought battles in federal district and appeals courts, as well as the Supreme Court, in an effort to obtain crucial documents that the committee needed to piece together Trump’s plans. He tapped prominent outside lawyers, including Supreme Court litigators Michael Dreeben and Neal Katyal, to support the House’s legal claims. The committee’s work led to a Supreme Court ruling that overrode Trump’s claim of executive privilege over his White House records, forced key allies to turn over massive tranches of emails and helped arm lawmakers with information that became the backbone of their case. Raskin, who helped run the Jan. 6 committee, said the panel’s experience is not replicable, in part because it operated, functionally, without a minority aiming to disrupt its carefully choreographed moves — the result of a GOP boycott. But he said the panel’s relatively uninhibited strategy provides lessons in how the House’s oversight operations can work in the new Congress. And given the huge margin Democrats expect next year, Raskin noted, Democrats will greatly outnumber Republicans on the House’s key investigative panels. Josh Gerstein, Riley Rogerson and Chris Marquette contributed to this report. CORRECTION: A previous version of this report misstated Scott Perry’s party affiliation.This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/11/democrats-house-counsel-donald-trump-investigations

item.title: Republicans block Hegseth impeachment push, but Democrats could try again in January
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Republican-controlled U.S. House of Representatives voted on Tuesday to effectively kill the articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth — for now — by blocking their consideration on the House floor and sending them back to the Judiciary Committee, where GOP leaders can hold them up until the next Congress is seated in January 2027. Democrats — who voted unanimously against shelving the impeachment charges — will have a large House majority next year after winning at least 255 seats in last week's midterm elections. They have already vowed to try to remove Hegseth from office when they take control of Congress. "In the majority, one of the first things we're gonna do is run Pete Hegseth out of town," Democratic Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the minority leader who is poised to become House speaker, said at a rally last month . Eleven Democrats missed Tuesday’s vote, which succeeded in blocking the charges by a 211 to 204 margin. Rep. Thomas Massie, a Republican from Kentucky, reintroduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Monday, alleging that the embattled Pentagon chief had committed "high crimes and misdemeanors" and abused the power of his office by violating the War Powers Resolution, conducting military operations without congressional authorization and ordering unlawful military actions in several countries. On Tuesday, Massie was the only Republican who broke with his party and voted to keep the articles of impeachment alive. Before Tuesday's vote, Hegseth struck a defiant tone in a Pentagon news briefing. He described the impeachment efforts as "a farce" and insisted that "none of these are high crimes or misdemeanors — they are partisan policy disagreements from people who want to politicize our military." He added, "That's what it is. Policy disagreements. Not high crimes. Not misdemeanors. Not treason. Not bribery. Not the kinds of offenses the founders intended when they wrote the impeachment clause." While Hegseth did not mention Massie by name, he criticized the actions of a "disgruntled congressman" and said the "proper remedy" for a policy disagreement was legislation. "It's a political spectacle," Hegseth said. "A personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment. Time for one man's final days in Congress to try to do damage to this president." He added, "This is not patriotism. This is sabotage." Related: Only 2 Cabinet officials have ever been impeached. Could Pete Hegseth be next? Hegseth also said the resolution suggested the U.S. would punish its own military for carrying out its job. "Let's be clear about what this resolution actually does," he said. "It tells our enemies — Iran, the cartels, every adversary watching — that the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership." President Trump celebrated Tuesday night's House vote on Truth Social , where he said that Democrats' attempt to impeach Hegseth "miserably FAILED!" Earlier in the day, Trump posted on Truth Social that Hegseth had earned an "'A' PLUS, PLUS, PLUS" for his defense against Massie, and described the defense secretary as "perhaps the most popular and successful military official in the Country," adding, "Pete Hegseth should be praised, not Impeached." Hegseth leaves a meeting of defense ministers in the Philippines on Oct. 28. Pool via Getty Images The expected impeachment filing came as Congress returned to Washington, D.C. , to begin a lame-duck session following the historic rout that the GOP suffered in last week's midterm elections . Hegseth has been facing intense political backlash over the United States' costly and unpopular war with Iran, which some top Republicans — including Trump — blame in part for the drubbing that cost them control of Congress. "Despite the absence of a declaration of war, specific statutory authorization, or a national emergency created by an attack upon the United States," Massie said in a speech on the House floor, "Secretary Hegseth knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders to initiate war against a foreign nation." Massie said Hegseth "has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law." His actions thus "warrant impeachment and trial, removal from office and disqualification to hold and enjoy any office of honor, trust or profit under the United States," the Kentucky Republican said. Earlier, Trump told CNN at a White House press conference he would "stand by him," saying that he believes Massie "has a lot of hatred in his heart." Massie — who in May lost his bid for reelection to Ed Gallrein, a Trump-backed challenger, in the GOP primary — first introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth in September. But House Speaker Mike Johnson later canceled the final scheduled voting day before the midterm recess, delaying a vote. It's unclear whether Massie's impeachment effort would have succeeded on the House floor under Republican control. Massie had previously told ABC News he was "confident" there would have been "enough GOP defectors for it to pass." Trump has repeatedly insisted that he is not considering replacing his Pentagon chief, at least not yet. "No, I think he's doing a very good job," Trump told reporters last week. The president also said he was unaware of a report that Hegseth has been quietly angling to fill the U.S. Senate seat that will be vacated by Tennessee GOP Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who was elected as the state's next governor. "I think he's doing a very good job, and I actually think he'd be very popular if he did that. But I haven't heard that at all," Trump said when asked if he would want the defense secretary to fill Blackburn's seat. CBS News , however, reported last week that Trump "has been asking advisers" whether he should stay or go. Hegseth, a former Fox News host who has served as defense secretary since January 2025, has been Trump's most visible cheerleader for the Iran war, which the U.S. and Israel initiated in February and which has led to surging oil prices. He has also been among the advisers urging Trump to restart the war. He and Adm. Brad Cooper, the head of U.S. Central Command, have supported a return to major combat operations against Iran during recent briefings on military options, the Wall Street Journal reported on Nov. 6, while Vice President JD Vance and special envoy Steve Witkoff have pushed for diplomacy to end the conflict. The U.S. Capitol building is seen in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 4. Kevin Carter/Getty Images Trump acknowledged on Nov. 4 that the Iran war had partly contributed to the midterm election rout that handed Democrats control of Congress. Vance was unequivocal. "The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone," Vance wrote in a lengthy post on X . "The reason we lost is the war." The vice president did not call out Hegseth by name. But other Republicans did. Sen. Thom Tillis, a Republican from North Carolina, told CBS News that Hegseth faces "a reckoning." "He is one of the reasons why we don't have the funding or guarantee for defense that we need," Tillis said on election night. "I think after the election, we need to determine whether or not he's the best person to bring those needs to Congress." Tillis, who voted to confirm Hegseth last year, recently called on Trump to fire him. "I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country," Tillis wrote in a scathing assessment of Hegseth on X in September. "He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and well-being of our fighting force. I urge the President to find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it." Rep. James Comer of Kentucky, the Republican chairman of the House Oversight Committee, said on Nov. 6 that "there's a lot of questions about Hegseth." "We have no idea what the strategy is moving forward in Iran," Comer told NewsNation . "No one's happy about Iran." A fire burns at an oil depot in Tehran, Iran, on March 8 after U.S. and Israeli attacks. Hassan Ghaedi/Anadolu via Getty Images When Democrats take control of both the House and Senate next year, they will have the ability to call for hearings and launch investigations into virtually any aspect of the Trump administration — and Hegseth's handling of the military is high on their list. Hegseth, for his part, has remained defiant. In a 5-and-a-half-minute video posted to X on Nov. 5, Hegseth defended the Iran war, touted changes he's implemented as Pentagon chief ("We ended the weird and the woke") and praised Trump's leadership while dismissing Massie's impeachment pursuit. "A disgruntled, defeated congressman along with all his Democrat allies has dropped sham impeachment articles against yours truly," Hegseth said. "It didn't work with President Trump and it won't work with me." This article originally appeared on Yahoo News at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/article/house-republicans-block-effort-to-impeach-hegseth-in-near-party-line-vote-231716935.html

item.title: Military-linked Chinese university bought Nvidia H200 chips despite U.S. blacklist
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Eduardo Baptista BEIJING, Nov 11 (Reuters) - A Chinese university with deep ties to the People's Liberation Army bought Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips last month despite being on a US export blacklist, procurement records show, highlighting gaps in Washington's efforts to curb China's access to advanced technology. The findings come as Nvidia and its CEO Jensen Huang face mounting scrutiny in Washington over his lobbying for looser restrictions on sales ‌of AI chips to China, following reports alleging he was targeted by a Chinese spying operation. Huang has argued that continued US sales to China would preserve American technological leadership and keep Chinese customers reliant on US technology. ‌But some US lawmakers say access to Nvidia's most powerful AI chips can speed China's development of AI systems for weapons design, intelligence analysis and military modernisation. Both Democrats and Republicans in Congress have urged stronger controls on China's access to advanced AI chips, such as chip-tracking requirements and greater congressional oversight ​of exports. Three Republican congressional committee chairmen have requested a briefing with Huang on November 18 over his reported contacts with an alleged Chinese intelligence operative. Northwestern Polytechnical University bought two H200 chips last month for 874,700 yuan ($123,000), according to an October 21 procurement record on its website. Northwestern is a member of the "Seven Sons of National Defense" group of Chinese universities under U.S. sanctions and with a history of conducting defence-related research for Beijing. The chips were purchased for its management school from Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology rather than directly from Nvidia, the record shows. The H200 is among Nvidia's most capable chips for training and running advanced AI systems and is subject to US export licence approvals, which are normally denied for blacklisted institutions such as Northwestern Polytechnical. Northwestern Polytechnical also bought access this year to ‌H200 chips and other powerful Nvidia AI processors through five contracts for rented computing capacity ⁠from Chinese companies, procurement records show. Reuters is reporting the chip purchases and computing contracts for the first time. Northwestern Polytechnical, Nvidia and the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, which oversees export controls, did not respond to requests for comment. Reuters could not determine contact details for Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology. TRADE BLACKLIST Based in the northwestern city of Xian, Northwestern Polytechnical conducts research related ⁠to military aircraft, missiles and satellites. The US Commerce Department added the university to its trade blacklist, known as the Entity List, in 2001 over its alleged involvement in missile-proliferation activities and military research. It tightened the restrictions in 2019, making licences for exports of controlled US technology to the university subject to a policy of denial in most circumstances. Northwestern Polytechnical's purchases show how Chinese institutions with military ties continue to obtain US AI computing power through domestic suppliers, either by buying chips outright or renting access to servers containing them. A Reuters review of ​26 ​Chinese procurement and corporate records from this year found universities and research institutions buying US-restricted Nvidia chips or renting access to Nvidia-powered computing services ​that use such chips through domestic suppliers. Several had close links to China's defence industry ‌or military research. The universities named in the records did not respond to requests for comment. NVIDIA CHIPS FOR MILITARY-LINKED RESEARCH US President Donald Trump's administration began allowing some H200 exports to China on a case-by-case basis in January. But that policy did not lift the separate restrictions applying to Entity List organisations such as Northwestern Polytechnical. The January licensing rules also require safeguards to prevent blacklisted entities and military end-users from remotely accessing chips exported under the policy, which covers H200 processors and less advanced models. In addition to the management school's outright purchase of the two H200 chips, procurement records show the university's cybersecurity school awarded two seven-month contracts in January for access to servers containing eight H200 chips each. The contracts, worth 441,700 yuan and 441,000 yuan, covered fine-tuning AI models and reinforcement-learning training. It also rented access to servers containing eight Nvidia A100 chips and eight A800 chips. The A100 and A800 are banned from export to all Chinese entities, though the H200 is the most advanced of those cited in Northwestern Polytechnical's ‌procurement records. In April, another university institute bought computing services requiring at least 24 A100 chips in a 375,000 yuan contract for structural and ​fluid-dynamics simulations. The awards went to several little-known Chinese technology suppliers. The records offered scant information about where the processors originated or where the rented servers ​operated. Under Chinese law, public procurement agencies must verify that suppliers can fulfil orders before announcing winning bidders and signing ​contracts. A WIDER MARKET The procurement records show a wider market for restricted Nvidia AI chips and computing services at Chinese universities. Shenzhen University bought three H100 processors, another high-end Nvidia AI chip banned by the ‌US, for 769,800 yuan in September. Wuhan University of Technology bought a server containing an ​H100 chip for 355,000 yuan in June and four A100 chips ​in a separate 344,000 yuan purchase, the records show. Beihang University, another of the Seven Sons of National Defense universities, bought four A800 processors for 489,000 yuan in April. Beihang has close ties to China's aerospace and defence industries and conducts research for military aviation and space programmes. Two government procurement announcements in July and September named suppliers selected to provide computing services using Nvidia H800 and A800 chips restricted from export to China to the University of ​Chinese Academy of Sciences. One listed H800 access at 10 yuan per chip-hour. A separate ‌January procurement award named a supplier of six A100 chips worth 484,800 yuan for a Shenzhen-based public institution. Reuters has previously reported that Chinese institutions acquired restricted Nvidia chips embedded in servers made by Super Micro ​Computer, Dell and Gigabyte through domestic resellers. Reuters has also documented an underground market in China for restricted Nvidia chips sourced from overseas inventories and third-country intermediaries. Last week, Reuters reported that small quantities of H200 ​chips had reached China through indirect routes while Beijing withheld approval for large-scale imports. (Reporting by Eduardo Baptista; Editing by Jamie Freed) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://finance.yahoo.com/news/exclusive-pla-linked-chinese-university-051308504.html

item.title: Trump's judicial confirmations to face resistance in Democratic-controlled Senate
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Washington — After seeing success in reshaping the federal judiciary in his first term and the initial two years of his second administration, President Trump and Republicans' campaign to shift the courts to the right could be coming to an end with Democrats poised to take control of the Senate next year. During his first term in office, Mr. Trump successfully put more than 230 judges on the federal bench, including three justices on the Supreme Court, remaking the judicial branch for decades. So far during his second term, the Senate has confirmed 57 of the president's judicial picks. In total, Trump nominees make up about one-third of active federal judges . But Democrats are now poised to control at least 54 Senate seats , and as many as 56 depending on the outcome of races in Mississippi and Alaska, making it unlikely that Mr. Trump will fill many more vacancies on the U.S. district and appeals courts. "No one, or nearly no one, is going to get confirmed, so what he does in terms of nominating people, we'll see," Ed Whelan, a distinguished senior fellow at the Ethics and Public Policy Center and former law clerk to the late Justice Antonin Scalia, told CBS News. There are currently 28 vacancies on the federal courts and another 15 seats that will open up in the coming weeks and months. So far, the president has formally sent to the Senate 16 nominees for those existing and future vacancies, though it's possible he submits more names for consideration before the current Congress finishes its work. Mr. Trump announced on Truth Social earlier Tuesday three more nominees to district courts in Texas and South Carolina. The GOP-led Senate Judiciary Committee is moving quickly to advance those picks before control of the upper chamber changes hands. It voted to advance four of the president's district court candidates and held confirmation hearings for four other judicial nominees Tuesday. The panel is expected to hold more confirmation hearings next week, a break from committee practice of holding those proceedings every other week, according to a source familiar with the panel's workings. Republicans are violating "numerous longstanding standards in a desperate attempt to confirm more than 30 qualified loyalists to lifetime appointments before Democrats take the majority," Sen. Dick Durbin, the top Democrat on the Judiciary Committee, said Tuesday. Durbin raised concerns about two of Mr. Trump's latest picks to serve as federal judges in Texas: James Sullivan, who lost his bid for reelection to the Texas Supreme Court last week, and T. Elliot Gaiser, the head of the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel whose only tie to Texas is a one-year clerkship for a judge on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit. The Judiciary panel received information from Sullivan after he lost his campaign for Texas Supreme Court justice last week and from Gaiser on Nov. 8, before the president announced his intent to nominate each man, according to the source. Both are slated to appear before senators for confirmation hearings next week. "There are many things we still can do, and I hope we'll use them. And one of them is not to expedite nominees who have not been carefully vetted," Durbin said. "I hope we don't accept that as a standard in this committee." But Sen. Chuck Grassley, an Iowa Republican who chairs the Judiciary Committee, pushed back on Durbin's claim that he is departing from its typical practices. He argued that there are no committee rules about how quickly it can move to hold confirmation hearings or when those proceedings are held, and said chairs have discretion to set the panel's schedule. "Historically, this committee has shortened timelines when circumstances warrant it," he said. In anticipation of Democratic control of the upper chamber, Republicans are expected to make judicial nominees a focus of the lame-duck period. "The priority is going to be getting the judges across the finish line," Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters Monday. But seats on the federal bench that remain open come the end of the current Congress are likely to remain unfilled for at least the next two years. "For the past two years, we've seen Trump seeking to stack our courts — district courts, circuit courts — with loyalists to him and not to the Constitution, and I think he's going to try to continue to do that," Rachel Rossi, president of the Alliance for Justice, a progressive judicial advocacy group, said. "In this moment, when Trump has clearly created this litmus test that there must be loyalty to him and not the Constitution, it's hard to see how Democrats can support nominees going forward." It is not unprecedented in the Senate for the party in control to stymie the nominations of a president in the opposing party. During the final two years of former President Barack Obama's administration, when Republicans held the Senate majority, just 20 of his nominees to the district and appeals courts were confirmed. Obama's final judicial confirmation came six months before the end of his second term. Among the candidates that did not get a vote from the GOP-led Senate was Merrick Garland, who was nominated to replace Scalia on the Supreme Court following his death in February 2016. "What we've seen is the federal courts being stacked with extremists and loyalists, and now Democrats have the power to stop the reshaping of our courts in a very dangerous direction," Rossi said. "I think there's increasing visibility on what judges mean and what these lifetime seats mean, and the hope is that Democrats use their power and stand against any further reshaping of our judiciary." Of the 43 current and future vacancies, Mr. Trump has not yet announced candidates for more than half of those seats. Many of those are in states that will be represented by either two Democratic senators or one Republican and one Democratic senator next year. Democrats could work with the White House to find consensus on candidates to serve on the district courts in their states, but it's unclear whether there is an appetite from either side to do so. "Republicans on the Senate Judiciary Committee and the Trump administration have gutted the committee's oversight and confirmation authority," Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, a Rhode Island Democrat who is expected to lead the panel next year, said in a statement. "There needs to be accountability for years of Republican bad behavior, and a hard reset on the nominations process next Congress." Democrats' rout of Republicans in last week's midterm elections also makes it unlikely a Supreme Court justice appointed by a GOP president steps down in the final two years of Mr. Trump's term, given that a successor would likely not clear the Senate. The president made a significant impact on the nation's highest court, appointing three of the nine justices. Among those was Justice Amy Coney Barrett, who filled Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg's seat following her death in September 2020, during Mr. Trump's first term. Justices Clarence Thomas, 78, and Samuel Alito, 76, are the two oldest members of the high court, but Alito told The Wall Street Journal in August, "I'm here for another term." Alito also told CBS News chief legal correspondent Jan Crawford last month that while he considered retirement earlier this year, he feels he can still make a contribution to the Supreme Court. With neither justice expected to step down during the lame-duck session, it could be several years before there is both a GOP president and Senate in place to confirm their potential successors on the Supreme Court, raising concerns among conservatives that a Democratic president and Senate could fill the seats of the influential conservative justices. "Trump has managed to put in jeopardy his biggest achievement," Whelan said. This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/trump-judicial-confirmations-democrats-senate/

item.title: Democrat Scott Colom's lead grows in Mississippi Senate race with certification days away
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Democrat Scott Colom's lead over Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith in the uncalled Mississippi Senate race grew to 3,041 votes on Wednesday, according to the Associated Press , as officials work to finalize the results. Outstanding ballots were due by Tuesday, Nov. 10; they are no longer being accepted. County clerks have until Nov. 13 to certify the election. And Colom's lead has widened almost every day since Election Day, when it stood at just 65 votes. Even though 98% of the vote is in, the AP has yet to call the race because the gap between Colom and Hyde-Smith remains narrow — just 0.32% of all ballots cast. Colom has continually expressed confidence that his campaign will prevail, flooding the airwaves and attending at least eight events over the last few days. "It's very clear the direction of this," he told reporters on Friday . "[Cindy Hyde-Smith] needs to answer questions. What is her path to victory? She doesn't have one." In contrast, Hyde-Smith had "not been seen publicly since she left her election night watch party just outside of Jackson," according to CNN . She returned to Washington, D.C. on Tuesday and told CBS that she was " feeling very optimistic ." Along with Alaska — which also remains too close to call — the outcome in Mississippi will determine whether Democrats can expand their new Senate majority beyond its current size (54 seats) by flipping even more red states than they already have . But Alaska was supposed to be a toss-up . Mississippi — one of the reddest states in the country — wasn't really on the national radar. President Trump won the state by 23 percentage points in 2024 — his third straight win there. Looking ahead to the 2026 Senate race, analysts said it was a "likely Republican" hold . Barely anyone bothered to poll it . Yet, here we are, with Colom edging Hyde-Smith as lawyers, operatives and legal observers descend on Mississippi to watch officials count every last ballot. How did the Mississippi Senate race get so close — and what happens next? Who is Scott Colom? Colom, 43, was born in Columbus, Miss., to two lawyers who also participated in politics. In 1987, his father, Wilbur, ran for state treasurer as a Republican; his mother, Dorothy, served as the first Black Chancery Court judge in their home district. Colom earned his JD from the University of Wisconsin in 2009 and went on to serve as the first Black justice court judge in Lowndes County, Miss., before becoming the first Black city prosecutor in Columbus. In 2015, Colom defeated a nearly 30-year incumbent to become the first Black district attorney elected in a majority-white voting district in Mississippi history. He has since prosecuted a number of high-profile murder and sexual assault cases. Colom gives an update about his Senate race on Nov. 4, 2026 in Jackson, Miss. Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images In 2022, President Joe Biden nominated Colom to serve as federal judge for the Northern District of Mississippi. Leading Magnolia State Republicans — including Sen. Roger Wicker and former Govs. Phil Bryant and Haley Barbour — backed Colom's nomination. "I have known two generations of the Colom family for over 20 years and believe Scott Colom possesses the discernment to be a fair and exemplary judge," Bryant told the New York Times . But Hyde-Smith blocked Colom's nomination in the Senate, citing support his 2015 campaign received from a political action committee funded by George Soros and claiming that he favored allowing transgender athletes to compete in girls' and women's sports. The White House characterized Hyde-Smith's concerns as " spurious ." In a letter to Hyde-Smith urging her to reconsider, Colom confirmed that he had signed a letter with other prosecutors condemning efforts to criminalize gender-affirming care for transgender people, but insisted that their joint statement "did not comment on legislation specifically related to participation in athletics." Colom also said he had not known about Soros's contributions to the Mississippi Safety and Justice PAC "until I read about them in my hometown paper." Colom's unsuccessful nomination was returned to Biden on Jan. 3, 2024. In September 2025, Colom announced his U.S. Senate candidacy. How Colom caught up Hyde-Smith, 67, is a former lobbyist and state legislator who was serving as Mississippi's agriculture and commerce commissioner when she was appointed to the U.S. Senate in 2018 following the resignation of Republican Sen. Thad Cochran. She won a 2018 special election and a 2020 full-term election, and she has served in the Senate ever since. There were signs before Election Day that Hyde-Smith might be vulnerable to "voter apathy," as one Mississippi State University political science professor recently put it . Sen. Wicker won reelection in 2024 by 25 points; Hyde-Smith's margin of victory in 2020 was less than half that. And while the only polls made public this cycle showed Hyde-Smith ahead , her leads were stuck in the single digits — no survey put her support above 50%. One April Democratic poll showed Hyde-Smith trailing a hypothetical "someone else" 33% to 53%. Hyde-Smith speaks at a campaign event in Corinth, Miss., on Oct. 26, 2026. Madison Thorn/Bloomberg via Getty Images Regardless, Hyde-Smith seemed content to coast to reelection, barely bothering to appear on the campaign trail. But Colom didn't have that luxury — and when he cut a viral campaign ad about beef prices in mid-October, the tide started to turn. Asked earlier this year about soaring costs, including the price of beef, Hyde-Smith told local TV station WLOX that "all commodities go through peaks and valleys," but "you have so many proteins to choose from." In the final weeks of the campaign, Colom seized on Hyde-Smith's remark about "proteins" to mock her with a spot featuring incredulous Mississippians grilling burgers, dining out and shopping for groceries — and saying they'd rather "pick another senator instead" (along with other, more colorful language). The video has since racked up nearly 14 million views on Colom's X account . When the ad took off, national Democrats sprang into action. The Senate Majority PAC poured $2.2 million into the race; Senate Democrats' campaign arm contributed another $500,000. Former President Barack Obama filmed an endorsement ad. Former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and Sens. Cory Booker of New Jersey and Raphael Warnock of Georgia rushed to Mississippi to rally with Colom. In response, Republicans were forced to play defense, sending Trump to Mississippi in the final days of the campaign (along with cash infusions of their own). She done lost her damn mind. pic.twitter.com/wHPt4PSAob — Scott Colom (@scott_colom) October 13, 2026 In the end, it wasn't enough to give Hyde-Smith a decisive victory on Election Day. When Trump came to Mississippi, Colom went to his event to talk to rally-goers about health care, grocery bills and gas prices. "I got the best message ever for Republican voters in Mississippi," he told CNN afterward. "I'm going to get you what you were promised in 2024. You were promised lower grocery prices on Day One. That's what I will fight for. You were promised no more endless wars. That's what I will fight for. You were promised the full and transparent release of the Epstein files. That's what I will fight for." According to preliminary New York Times estimates , Colom performed 19 points better among white Mississippi voters than Harris, the 2024 Democratic presidential nominee. He won new voters — that is, those who didn't vote in 2024 — by 25 points. What happens next The contest between Colom and Hyde-Smith hasn't been called yet because officials are still tallying two remaining batches of ballots. The first batch contains mail-in absentee ballots, which had to arrive by Tuesday, Nov. 10. The other batch contains affidavit ballots, which were generally cast by people who did not present an acceptable photo ID at the polls or who had been marked as inactive on voter rolls. Voters also had until 5 p.m. local time on Tuesday, Nov. 10, to validate their affidavit ballots with an acceptable ID. County clerks in Mississippi now have until Friday, Nov. 13, to certify the election. The Colom campaign has said that roughly 15,000 affidavit ballots were cast this year. Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson said late last week that there were as many as 20,000 outstanding ballots of all kinds ; on Monday, he said more than 15,000 affidavit ballots had been processed and roughly 2,500 mail ballots were still expected to come in. Colom's team believes his lead will expand once all the outstanding ballots are counted. (It has already grown by nearly 3,000 votes since Election Day.) Ahead of Mississippi's March primaries, incorrect Experian information mistakenly led to the inactivation of legitimate voters — and inactivations have more than doubled in some jurisdictions since then. Discrepancies caused confusion and long lines at polling places on Election Day, forcing affected voters to cast affidavit ballots. The post-election process of validating, or “curing,” affidavit ballots has proven cumbersome as well . "We are going to make sure every single vote has been counted, and I am confident we will ultimately flip this seat," Colom wrote on X on last week . The next day he added that "my campaign, alongside the [Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee] and Elias Law Group, Lisa Ross, and our great team of local attorneys, are leading the effort to ensure every eligible voter is heard." Hyde-Smith also expressed confidence on Election Night. "We still don't have all the votes in, so we're not calling all of it tonight, but we're in a very good lead and I assure you, I will continue to be your U.S. Senator," she told supporters at the time. Last week, Mississippi Republican Party chairman Mike Hurst said he was "enthusiastic about these outstanding ballots because a number of these, a significant number of these, we believe, are in and remain in Republican-leaning districts, precincts and counties throughout the state." Mississippi is the only state in the country without a recount law. But if the margin is still razor-close, Colom or Hyde-Smith could challenge certain ballots in court. That would likely happen after certification on Nov. 13. Lawyers for Hyde-Smith and her campaign have formally written to Mississippi state officials to demand "the immediate separation, secure custody, and preservation of all affidavit ballots," according to the New York Times — a signal that they may pursue litigation if those ballots put Colom over the top. Hurst added last week that lawyers aligned with Hyde-Smith "will be ready, if necessary, to avail ourselves of every legal option at our disposal, if there is evidence that the law has been violated." For now, Hyde-Smith told reporters on Capitol Hill Tuesday that “votes should be counted, and that’s all we’re concentrating on today.” She added: “We’re just looking for the conclusion of our race.” This article originally appeared on Yahoo News at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/article/mississippi-senate-latest-scott-coloms-lead-over-cindy-hyde-smith-tops-3000-votes-as-deadline-looms-150352218.html

item.title: Jim Jordan looks to move Republicans beyond midterm rout
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
House Republicans on Tuesday tapped Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) to lead their diminished conference in the next Congress, betting that a conservative spitfire — and onetime leadership nemesis — can restore the fight to a party battered by the midterms and scrambling for a path back to power. In brief comments right out of the gate, Jordan set the tenor of the coming clash, vowing to fight the ascendant Democrats on the size and scope of federal power — an issue that’s taken on fresh significance with the arrival of a new crop of democratic socialist members. “When Democrats offer more government, we'll offer more freedom,” Jordan told reporters in the Capitol shortly after his victory at a press conference where new leaders declined to take questions. “And we will bring that fight in committee, on the floor and on the stump every single day." He has a steep climb ahead. Jordan’s task is not only to bring together the warring factions of a restive party demoralized by their election rout and sniping over who’s to blame but also to craft a message that will resonate with alienated voters ahead of the 2028 elections — all while defending President Trump from the myriad investigations the Democrats are promising into the president’s family, allies and administration. It was the size of the election losses, some Republicans said, that tipped the scales toward Jordan over Rep. Steve Scalise (R-La.), the outgoing majority leader whose many years in the leadership ranks became a liability, rather than an asset, after the midterm landslide. “He represents change,” said Rep. Darin LaHood (R-Ill.). “He also has a very detailed plan on how we get out of the minority. He has excellent communication skills. He's viewed as a fighter, which he is, and I think the conference was ready for a different direction.” “If the election would have been closer last week,” he added, “I think the results could have been different today.” For Jordan, the ascension represents an extraordinary arc for a right-wing renegade who built a brand in the Capitol for taking on party leaders, not joining their ranks. The Ohio Republican is a co-founder of the far-right House Freedom Caucus, a bloc of iconoclastic conservatives who have routinely butted heads with GOP leadership over government spending and, at times, blocked Republican legislation in an effort to yank the party further to the right. He is also chair of the House Judiciary Committee, a role he’s used to launch investigations into Democrats and other Trump political opponents. “Jim Jordan is a fighter. I think he doesn't mind saying the hard things, but he's level-headed, and he's going to be able to work with a lot of different personalities to stay focused on the mission and get the job done,” Rep. Sheri Biggs (R-S.C.) said. If Tuesday’s leadership elections were a referendum on the midterm results, however, they also didn’t supply the “clean slate” some GOP lawmakers were hoping for. Rep. Tom Emmer (Minn.), the Republican whip, fended off a challenge from Rep. August Pfluger (R-Texas) to keep his post. And Rep. Lisa McClain (Mich.), the GOP conference chair, will also remain in place after beating back challenges from Republican Reps. Greg Steube (Fla.) and Erin Houchin (Ind.). “This Republican leadership team will expose the Democrats’ lies and show the American people their true colors as the radical communists that they are,” Emmer said after his win. Trump stayed out of the leadership races — an unusual move for a president who has exerted his influence in past contests. Many Republicans are blaming Trump’s policies — particularly the Iran war, global tariffs and a deportation surge — for dragging down GOP candidates in the midterms. Some even suggested they chose Jordan because he expressed a willingness to break from the president on certain issues. Rep. Rich McCormick (R-Ga.) said he asked Jordan what the Republican conference was going to do “now that we have to deal with a president who we're not sure … how he's going to go forward.” “I thought he gave a very good answer, which was instead of waiting to see what the president’s going to say, we lead. We lead with a message based on what we want to say, and that's what I've always tried to do myself. I mean, each individual has to know their individual district as well as possible,” McCormick said. “We’re independent thinkers, right? … I want to not worry about what the president says. I want to have my own opinion, and … what's funny is the president usually comes around to what I believe anyway. And if he doesn't, that's OK because we're not a cult. If everybody in the church agrees with everything the minister says, you're in a cult. We are not a cult. It's very high time to realize that. And it goes back to the Reagan rule, right? It's OK if you disagree with me on a certain percentage. We can still be on the same team,” he added. The leadership transition, from Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) to Jordan, could not offer a more stark contrast in styles and personas. Johnson is a constitutional lawyer, prim and bespectacled, who often quotes Bible verses and borrowed church terminology in pledging to be a “servant leader.” Jordan is a former champion wrestler, still fit and muscular, who’s known for eschewing a blazer around the Capitol and jousting routinely with Democrats from his perch atop the Judiciary Committee. The House Freedom Caucus repeatedly tried to tap Jordan to run against former Speaker Kevin McCarthy (R-Calif.), which he resisted. But after McCarthy was ousted, it spurred a contentious 2023 battle for the Speakership between Scalise and Jordan. Scalise initially won the Republican nomination for Speaker then, defeating Jordan in a secret-ballot vote. But, he later withdrew from the race when it became clear he would not win enough support to secure the gavel. Jordan was later chosen as the nominee for Speaker, but he repeatedly fell short of the votes needed to clinch the post. “It's almost like this is the right time for him,” Rep. Tom Cole (Okla.), a member of the House Republican Steering Committee and the top Republican on the House Appropriations Committee, told reporters after the vote. “I think we need, you know, a combat guy, so to speak. But he's as good at political combat as anybody I've ever seen. So I think he'll do an excellent job for us.” Rep. Nicole Malliotakis (R-N.Y.) also said she sees Jordan as a unifier despite his staunch conservatism. “Jim Jordan is somebody who's a fighter, somebody who's thoughtful when he speaks,” she said. “He's eloquent. He doesn't miss a beat. He's out there talking about the issues, talking about what people are thinking. I think he'll do a good job. Look, I'm one of the more centrist members. … He brings everybody together.” “I think the reason I had supported him for Speaker two years ago, I thought he was the one who could bring everybody together because he had relationships with more moderate members, with the Freedom Caucus folks, and everybody in between,” she added. “So I think you know he handles himself in a way that he can get the job done.” Congressional Democrats were quick to criticize the pick as another instance of the GOP conference committing itself to a far-right pick after an election that they view as a resounding rejection of Trump. “Stephen Miller and Jim Jordan,” Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) wrote on social media, noting the promotion of Trump’s White House adviser to chief of staff. “Republicans learned absolutely nothing from what happened a week ago, and are responding by elevating their most extreme voices to positions of power.” But GOP members defended the choice. “I think you look at our conference, we're a significantly more conservative conference than what we were coming into this,” Rep. Brian Mast (R-Fla.) said, referencing the number of moderate members who lost their reelection bids. “And I think if you look at that, you're going to see us push our conservative values.” Rep. Michael Cloud (R-Texas), a member of the House Freedom Caucus, asserted voters still wanted Trump’s agenda and said he also saw Jordan as a figure who could fight any eventual impeachment effort that Democrats might bring against Trump. “He's a conservative. He's also a smart strategist. He's definitely a good communicator, and especially where we're headed with the Dems, who seem obsessed with impeachment and, you know, shenanigans, he's had to lead the defense on that before,” Cloud said. “So I think we'll be well prepared headed into the future.” Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. All rights reserved. This material may not be published, broadcast, rewritten, or redistributed. For the latest news, weather, sports, and streaming video, head to The Hill. This article originally appeared on The Hill at https://thehill.com/the-120/6212145-jim-jordan-house-gop-future-midterms/

item.title: Joe Biden says he wouldn't have run in 2024 if he'd known he had cancer
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
NEED TO KNOW Joe Biden gets candid about his stage 4 prostate cancer as he releases his new memoir , Promise Me, America The former president reflects on life, withdrawing from the 2024 race and the legacy he hopes to leave Dr. Jill Biden describes the daily realities of caring for her husband with support from their family Two days after the Democrats swept the midterm elections , former President Joe Biden has that signature twinkle in his blue eyes. “Look at the people we got elected: first women governors, first Black governors,” he tells PEOPLE with a quiet rasp. At 83, and living with stage 4 prostate cancer — for which he completed radiation and is undergoing hormone therapy — Biden is slower than when he suddenly withdrew from the presidential race in 2024 following a disastrous debate against Donald Trump and amid concerns about his health. Still, his perennial optimism remains. “I’m not saying I’ll live forever,” says the one-term president, seated in the dining room of his Wilmington, Del., lake house, “but the point is that I have all my faculties, I have access to all the things I had before and I feel good.” Former President Joe Biden in his study at home in Wilmington, Del., on Nov. 5. Credit: Victoria Will He’s fighting the disease “like hell,” Biden writes in his presidential memoir, Promise Me, America , out Nov. 17. Through it all, his wife, Dr. Jill Biden , 75, has been by his side. Being a family caregiver — like 63 million Americans — is “emotionally, physically hard,” the former first lady says after returning home from volunteering at a women’s prison, where she teaches literature part-time. Although she has help looking after her husband and says family is a constant at the house, “My days are making sure he eats right. Does he exercise? Is he taking the right medicine? Did I talk to the doctor?” Reality came into focus when she read a magazine at a nail salon and imagined traveling to the destinations on the glossy pages. “All of a sudden it struck me, like, ‘Wait a minute, this isn’t our life now,’ ” she says. “We’re on a new journey.” With no questions off the table, President Biden addresses his life and health now, his presidency and the legacy he hopes to leave behind. In May 2025, 118 days after you left office, you announced that you had been diagnosed with stage 4 prostate cancer that had spread to your bones. You write that you’re fighting it with the “help of an incredible medical team and an even better family.” What does that fight look like? It looks very positive. There’s a lot of people who’ve been diagnosed with cancer, particularly the kind of cancer I have, who live long lives, who live for another 10, 20 years. And so far, the two tests that have been done show that the cancer is not metastasized beyond what it already was ... There are eight different pills I take a day. Former President Joe Biden at home in Wilmington, Del., on Nov. 5, 2026 Credit: Victoria Will Next June will mark your 50th wedding anniversary. What has cancer taught you about your marriage that you didn’t know before? Nothing. I knew from the beginning what she was. Jill is, first of all, bright as hell. Secondly, I think she’s the most beautiful woman in the world, which every husband probably thinks, but I believe it. And we have a real partnership. Joe Biden and wife Jill Biden pose for a photo together with their cat in May 2025. Credit: Joe Biden/X How has your family, including your grandchildren and your great-grandchild, supported you? They’re always here. “Can we come up, Pop? Pop, can we do this?” I do more with my grandchildren than I do with anybody else, and that’s for real. I’m interested and they’re interested in serious things as well ... They’re involved in a lot of things having to do with public service. They participate in a number of issues that relate to the well-being of the country. They’re the loves of my life. The Biden family celebrated Easter 2026 in Santa Ynez, California As the second Catholic to become president, you’ve been candid about how your faith has guided you through hard times. Do you still see signs of those you’ve lost? I do. I see signs of their love in their progeny. I see signs of their love of things that I find out that they have done that I didn’t know they had done before ... My son Hunter , he and his brother Beau were born a year and a day apart. They’re each other’s best friends in the world. When Beau died, it was a blow to Hunter in a way that was almost beyond repair ... Now he’s deeply involved in public policy things. He’s deeply involved in making the case, but he’s straight as an arrow in terms of his alcoholism. My dad used to have an expression: “Joey, family’s the beginning, the middle and the end.” And that’s how it is. You write, “People say I was deluding myself that I could do the job [of president] at my age. My answer to that is: I was doing the job.” Why do you think they felt that way? It’s natural. If tomorrow you’re going to say that the head of your [company] is going to be hired on as an 80-year-old person, you go, “What the hell’s going on?” But the value I think I brought was I knew so many of the leaders, I knew their inclinations, I knew what was going on, and many of them came to me. I thought it was value added, not subtracted. Standard medical guidelines don’t recommend routine prostate cancer screenings for men over 70. You write, “I was treated no differently from any other 82-year-old man in America. Maybe I should have been.” What do you say to Americans who believe that a screening should have been part of your annual physical? Look, White House doctors are doing what the whole entire medical profession is doing ... I had some discomfort, and Jill thought, Why isn’t that test done for men who are in their 70s? And there wasn’t any particular [sign] except recurring pain. When he wasn’t downing a black-and-white milkshake, former President Joe Biden chatted with diners at the Charcoal Pit in Wilmington, Del., his favorite diner since high school, on Nov. 5. Credit: Victoria Will You describe a “cynical twist” on your cancer news: that some folks said you hid your cancer as president. Why do you think they reacted that way? A lot of people do that. They hide bad news from the public if they’re elected officials. I didn’t do that. We let the public know when I found out, when I knew what was going on. I think it’s important for a national leader, as president, to let people know they go through some of the very same things that a lot of American people are going through ... I wasn’t hiding it at all. Many have spoken about the toll of the Presidency. How might your undiagnosed cancer have exacerbated that? First of all, I never felt the toll. I read [others] like Harry Truman talk about [how] it’s the most difficult job in the world. I didn’t find it that way. And so I, quite frankly, found that it didn’t in any way interfere with my job. Former President Joe Biden in his study at home in Wilmington, Del., on Nov. 5 Credit: Victoria Will What do you miss the most about the job? The staff, the people in the White House. They’re good people, from the people making sure there’s a sheet on the bed to the people who are taking care of all the visitors that come through. They all have a sense of honor, what they’re doing in the White House. It’s the People’s House. What’s your reaction to the Trump ballroom and the East Wing being destroyed? Almost as disturbing as the gold bars on the walls of the White House and the Oval Office. I mean, what the hell are we talking about? I find it disturbing ... I’ve viewed the president’s judgment in tearing down the East Wing and a number of other things as nothing more than to try to create monuments to himself: “I built that.” I find it beneath the country. After Donald Trump defeated Kamala Harris in 2024, he and Melania returned to the White House on Jan. 20, 2025. Credit: Jim WATSON/AFP/Getty It’s been two years and four months since that debate moment on the stage with Trump. What is your perspective on it now? Look, I don’t know anybody who hasn’t made a mistake in a debate. To me, it was not very consequential. First of all, I thought there’d be another debate, which there wasn’t. But notwithstanding the fact that there wasn’t another debate, it didn’t disturb me because it wasn’t consequential. Former President Joe Biden chatted with staff at the Charcoal Pit, his favorite diner since high school, in Wilmington, Del., on Nov. 5. Credit: Victoria Will In hindsight, looking at the 2024 election, is there anything you would’ve done differently? What I can’t say, because there’s no evidence of it — if I had known that I was feeling lousy because I had cancer, I would have resigned. I would’ve not gone forward, because I don’t think an 80-year-old man with cancer should be running for [president]. But that wasn’t the case ... I believe that on an objective basis, I was the best-equipped person to do the job. Hunter has been speaking out on podcasts and social media. What do you make of that? Hunter is one of the brightest men I know. He has more moral and physical courage than most people I know, and I’m really proud of him. He’s making the case as to how we should proceed as a country. He’s said of the pardon you gave him: “Was it good for our Constitution? Was it good for the American people? Was it good for my father’s legacy? No on all accounts.” What’s your perspective? I disagree ... I watched the modus operandi of Trump. He goes after people without any basis, whether they’re viewed as an enemy. I knew what he would do. If I hadn’t pardoned — not just some of my family members, anyone who’s dealt with me—he would go back and try to do harm to them, as I’ve observed. Never miss a story — sign up for PEOPLE’s free daily newsletter to stay up-to-date on the best of what PEOPLE has to offer, from celebrity news to compelling human interest stories. In your book, for the first time, you share the letter that Trump left you in the Oval Office after you beat him in the 2020 election. Your takeaway: “It was almost as if there were two Donald Trumps.” What do you mean? That could have been written by President Kennedy to me or by President Johnson or by George Bush. I mean, it was gracious, it was generous, and it was totally inconsistent with the kind of president he’d been. Joe Biden’s new book, “Promise Me, America,” out Nov. 17 You write, “Promise me, America, that we will be the nation we know in our hearts we can be and should be.” What does that nation mean to you at 83, after more than 50 years of public service? It means to continue to hold those truths to be self-evident, that we’re all created equal. I got involved in politics because of the Civil Rights movement. It means to be engaged in trying to help make the country a better place than it has been, to give people the benefit of the doubt ... When I say, “Promise me, America,” I mean, America, you know the promises we made. Let’s keep them. Joe Biden was sworn in on his family Bible when he became president on Jan. 20, 2021. Credit: Kent Nishimura/Los Angeles Times/Getty How do you want the American people to remember you? I tell you, it’s the greatest honor any man or woman could be given anywhere to be the President of the United States of America. And I hope I kept the promise of America ... I didn’t say I didn’t make mistakes—but I meant what I said, and I did what I said I was going to do. PEOPLE VIPs can read our full conversation with Joe Biden in this week’s issue, available right now in the app . Read the original article on People This article originally appeared on People at https://people.com/joe-biden-new-interview-video-exclusive-12247044

item.title: JFK's family sues Trump over arch they say would cast a shadow on late president's grave
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Several members of the Kennedy family have sued President Donald Trump , aiming to stop the building of the triumphal arch he hopes to build near Washington, D.C., new court filings show. The proposed 250-foot monument in the style of Paris’ Arc de Triomphe would be built on the Virginia side of the Potomac River between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery, where American veterans have been laid to rest since the Civil War. According to Kennedy family members behind the lawsuit, the 25-story arch would "cast a shadow" over memorials to their family members laid to rest in the historic burial site. "President Donald J. Trump is attempting to unlawfully erect a massive arch," says the Kennedy family members’ lawsuit, "that will permanently cast shadows over and damage historically significant sightlines to the existing gravesites and memorials established in the Kennedy family’s honor at Arlington National Cemetery, as well as to the memorials of hundreds of thousands of fallen American heroes." According to the lawsuit, the arch would block sightlines onto the John F. Kennedy Eternal Flame, a memorial to the former president who was assassinated in 1963 . They contend it will also cast a shadow over the graves of prominent Kennedys buried in the cemetery. In addition to JFK, others buried there include Robert F. Kennedy, the former senator assassinated in 1968 , and Sen. Edward "Ted" Kennedy, who died in 2009 after 43 years of serving in Congress. Among the nine Kennedys named as plaintiffs in the lawsuit are RFK’s daughter Kerry Kennedy and Edward M. Kennedy, Jr. "Vanity should never stand in the way of valor," Kerry Kennedy, president of the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center, said in a statement following the court filing in Washington, D.C. A White House spokesperson in a statement slammed efforts to block construction of "this magnificent Arch." "It is unfortunate to see that some members of the Kennedy family have joined the litigation against the Arch as the project is intended to honor our heroes who rest in Arlington Cemetery," said White House spokesperson Davis Ingle. "The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation. We will continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds." USA TODAY has reached out to Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. for comment. Trump has previously promoted the project as both a landmark and a military asset. Speaking on Nov. 2 during an event highlighting improvements to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, he said the arch could house drones and snipers. "It's right smack in the middle of everything, so very important for our military. But from a beautification standpoint, it'll be the most beautiful arch in the world," Trump said. The court filing is the latest attempt to thwart the president’s attempt to build the arch. Opponents have previously argued that the arch would obstruct the view from the Lincoln Memorial to Arlington Cemetery, which was built on the confiscated land of former Confederate General Robert E. Lee. The clear view between the two sites is meant to represent the reunification of the country following the Civil War, according to court filings. Plans to build Trump’s arch have been approved by a board led by people appointed by the president. But other hurdles remain. A federal judge on Nov. 5 temporarily blocked the project from going forward in response to a separate lawsuit brought by Washington and Virginia, arguing that the president needs approval from Congress in order to build. Trump's plans to remake the nation's capital, including the proposed arch, are not popular among Americans. In May, polls showed 52% of Americans were against the project, including 41% who strongly oppose it, while only 21% of people support the plan to build the towering arch. Democrats retaking Congress in the midterms argued in the run-up to the election that the president was too focused on construction projects in Washington and not focused enough on bringing down the cost of living for everyday Americans. "I don't know if you've noticed, but he is very focused on home renovation. He should be on HGTV," former President Barack Obama quipped in one viral campaign moment. "Guy is building a ballroom that is bigger than the White House, paved over the Rose Garden – paved it over – put a helicopter pad on the side lawn." item.title: Nearly one in five food stamp recipients could lose benefits under Trump proposal
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A SNAP sign is seen at the entrance to a Big Lots store in Portland, Oregon. - iStock Editorial/Getty Images Roughly 6.3 million low-income Americans could lose their food stamp benefits in fiscal year 2029 under a US Department of Agriculture proposed rule released Tuesday. That’s nearly one in five enrollees in the safety net program. The proposal would end a policy that gives states flexibility in approving applicants for food stamps if they are receiving other public aid, which could have higher gross income limits. The policy, known as “broad-based categorical eligibility,” has long been a target of Republicans. The affected food stamp recipients would no longer qualify because their income or resources exceed federal limits for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, the formal name for food stamps, according to the proposed rule. The move would also have ripple effects across other key nutrition assistance programs, particularly those for children. About 1.8 million children would no longer be automatically eligible for free school meals if the proposal is finalized, though the USDA said nearly all would still qualify for free or reduced-price meals if they apply separately. Similarly, 16,500 pregnant women, mothers, infants and children would have to apply for the WIC nutrition program, while another 5,500 participants would no longer be eligible for it. The proposed rule would increase the paperwork burden on enrollees and on state agencies, which could ensnare some eligible participants and lead to their losing benefits, advocates said. Some families, particularly those with immigrant members, are afraid to fill out government paperwork and call attention to themselves. “Instead of helping families, the administration is making life harder for them,” said Gina Plata-Nino, SNAP policy & advocacy director at the Food Research & Action Center. “These are working families.” Also, the USDA stopped measuring food insecurity last year, which makes it harder to keep track of Americans’ ability to feed themselves and their families, said Ali Hard, policy director at the National WIC Association. The USDA defended the proposed rule, noting it would reduce federal spending on SNAP by nearly $45 billion and state spending by $5.2 billion over five years. “Broad-based categorical eligibility has bloated the welfare rolls for decades. It has allowed States to take short cuts, error rates to balloon, and those with income and assets far above federal limits access to a benefit meant for the neediest among us,” the agency said in a statement. “Correcting this loophole is long overdue.” The proposed rule comes at a time when SNAP enrollment has plummeted by more than 5 million people — including an estimated 2 million children — since President Donald Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in July 2025, according to the left-leaning Center on Budget and Policy Priorities. Advocates attribute the drop to states’ implementing stricter eligibility reviews to avoid payment error penalties and other provisions in the package. The Trump administration proposed a similar rule ending “broad-based categorical eligibility” in 2019, but it was withdrawn by the Biden administration in 2021. item.title: Top White House lawyer warns Dems that threats of oversight could be criminally probed
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned probes into the Trump administration, going as far as claiming that such investigations — a standard oversight function of Congress -- may amount to “blatant criminality.” White House counsel Will Scharf issued the warning in a letter dated Monday to Rep. Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee. Garcia most likely would chair the powerful panel in the new Democratic-controlled Congress that is seated in January. Garcia warned Trump officials to “lawyer up” after his party’s stunning victories in last week's midterm elections. In response, Scharf wrote in Monday’s letter that “threats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality." The letter’s existence was first reported by Punchbowl News. Garcia said in response to the letter that “it appears Donald Trump has something to hide” and stressed that Congress’s investigative powers do not need the “permission of the White House.” “Congress has wide latitude to conduct investigations and oversight, an authority inherent in the power to legislate,” Garcia said. “The American people voted overwhelmingly for us to pass laws to root out corruption and abuse.” Democrats are preparing a vast oversight agenda to look at how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office. The Republican president and his White House have long denied any wrongdoing. Garcia also wants to look at the administration’s handling of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation and Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations . Other targets include Trump’s White House ballroom and other construction projects, as well as the Trump family’s role in mineral deals and Trump’s crypto dealings with special envoy Steve Witkoff. Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a CNN interview that aired Sunday that “there could be” a crime to investigate if rhetoric from Democrats turned threatening. He appeared to strike a more conciliatory tone during an appearance in Missouri this week, saying “Congress has oversight authority. It always has, it always will. The Department of Justice, the federal government, works with Congress to address questions they have — whether it’s through subpoenas or letters — so we’re not going to stop working with Congress.” “Nothing I’ve said this weekend, or in the past, should suggest otherwise,” he added. ___ Associated Press writer Eric Tucker contributed.
